findings.claim: All 48 practice questions are labelled “20 marks — Extract Analysis”.
findings.truth: The 19th-century prose question is worth 40 marks (20% of the GCSE). Relabelled 40 marks on all 48 questions.

findings.claim: All 48 mark schemes read ‘Top band (17–20) … Band 4–1: Progressively less detailed.’
findings.truth: Ladder is scaled to 20 marks and uses invented band numbers. Rescaled to five equal house bands over 40: Top 33–40, Upper-mid 25–32, Mid 17–24, Lower-mid 9–16, Low 1–8.
findings.evidence: House rule for malformed ladders; mark total from spec §2.2.

findings.claim: “Key themes of Jane Eyre with exam strategy for Eduqas Component 2 Section B.”
findings.truth: Names the board (house rule forbids it in prose) and uses banned component/section codes. Rewritten as ‘the 19th-century novel question’ (79 chars).
findings.evidence: House rule (Eduqas/WJEC neutral phrasing); CHECK_PROMPT banned-string list.

findings.claim: “For the 40-mark Eduqas question, embed AO1–AO4 in every paragraph…”
findings.truth: Section B assesses AO1, AO2 and AO3 only. AO4 (written accuracy / SPaG) is not assessed on the 19th-century prose question. Board name also removed.
findings.evidence: spec §2.2: ‘Section B assesses AO1, AO2 and AO3.’ (AO4 sits in Section A and Component 1 Section A.)

findings.claim: “You will be assessed against the standard GCSE English Literature assessment objectives — AO1 … AO2 … AO3 (context), and AO4 (written accuracy).”
findings.truth: Only AO1, AO2 and AO3 are assessed here; spelling and grammar carry no marks on this question.

findings.claim: Key fact: “assessed against four AOs … Top-band responses embed all four within every paragraph”.
findings.truth: The qualification has four AOs, but this question is marked on the first three only. Reworded to keep the four-AO framing and name the three that count here.

findings.claim: “How many AOs does the Eduqas prose question assess?”, correct index 2 = ‘Four’.
findings.truth: The answer is Three. The key marked the true answer wrong. Question stem also named the board; both q and correct fixed (correct → 1).
findings.evidence: spec §2.2: ‘Section B assesses AO1, AO2 and AO3.’

findings.claim: “Aim for 4–5 developed paragraphs in 45 minutes.”
findings.truth: The section is one of three equal 40-mark sections in a 2 hour 30 minute paper, so about 50 minutes.
findings.evidence: spec §2.2: Component 2 written examination 2 hours 30 minutes; three sections at 20% each.

findings.claim: Quotation bank ends: ‘“Reader, I married him” (agency), “” (Rochester’s growth). Learn them all.’ — an empty quotation.
findings.truth: Filled with a verified line: ‘I thank my Maker, that, in the midst of judgment, he has remembered mercy.’

findings.claim: Helen Burns ‘tells Jane: “We shall be recognised… by the God of all.”’
findings.truth: Fabricated. Helen says ‘You will come to the same region of happiness: be received by the same mighty, universal Parent, no doubt, dear Jane.’ Her last words are ‘Good-night, Jane.’

findings.claim: Flashcard [3] answer: ‘We shall be recognised... by the God of all.’
findings.truth: Same fabricated quotation; replaced with the ch.9 wording.

findings.claim: Flashcard [10]: ‘Helen Burns — dies at Lowood saying ‘We shall be recognised... by the God of all.’’
findings.truth: Same fabricated quotation. Helen’s last words are ‘Good-night, Jane.’

findings.claim: Rochester’s respect for Jane is evidenced by ‘“the liveliness of your mind”’, and flashcard [11] asks for ‘the Rochester compliment that mirrors Darcy’s attraction in Pride and Prejudice’.
findings.truth: ‘The liveliness of your mind’ is Darcy to Elizabeth in Pride and Prejudice ch.60. The word ‘liveliness’ does not appear anywhere in Jane Eyre. The flashcard is a line from a different text. Replaced with Rochester ch.23: ‘I ask you to pass through life at my side—to be my second self, and best earthly companion.’
findings.evidence: grep ‘liveliness’ on the Gutenberg text: 0 hits; ch.23 line 11700.

findings.claim: Jane paces ‘the third floor — directly above the room where Bertha is imprisoned’; ‘caged beneath her feet’; flashcard ‘Bertha is imprisoned directly below’.
findings.truth: Bertha is kept in a third-storey room off the very corridor Jane paces — the same floor, not below it. Reworded to ‘the same corridor’.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg ch.12 line 4930 (‘the corridor of the third storey’); ch.27 line 14292 (‘that third-storey room’).

findings.claim: ‘a distinct, formal, mirthless laugh’ given as a quotation.
findings.truth: The text reads ‘It was a curious laugh; distinct, formal, mirthless.’ Wording restored so a student quoting it is accurate.

findings.claim: Flashcard [6]: ‘What is Rochester’s manipulative strategy in Act 2 of Jane’s stay?’
findings.truth: Jane Eyre is a novel; it has no acts. Reworded to ‘during Jane’s time at Thornfield’.

findings.claim: Jane ‘divides the inheritance equally among all four cousins’ / ‘among the four Rivers cousins’.
findings.truth: Jane has three Rivers cousins (St John, Diana, Mary). The £20,000 is split four ways — Jane keeps £5,000 and each cousin gets £5,000.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg ch.33 line 17884: ‘nephew and three nieces of our uncle, will give five thousand to each’.

findings.claim: Flashcard [1]: ‘Which Jane line conveys the supernatural call from Rochester?’ — answer ‘Jane! Jane! Jane!’
findings.truth: The cry is Rochester’s, heard by Jane; it is not a line of Jane’s. Stem reworded.

findings.claim: ‘Jane feels herself being “gathered under a spell” by his influence.’
findings.truth: Not in the text. Brontë writes ‘I fell under a freezing spell’ (and later ‘rivet the spell’). Replaced with the real wording.

findings.claim: ‘he dies as a missionary, “sure of his reward.”’
findings.truth: The novel closes with St John alive but near death; Jane writes that ‘he anticipated his sure reward, his incorruptible crown’. The quoted phrase is a paraphrase.

findings.claim: ‘Jane tells St John: “If I join St John, I abandon half _____.”’
findings.truth: This is Jane’s private reflection in ch.34, not something she says to him. Stem reworded to ‘Jane reflects on St John’s offer’.

findings.claim: The final paragraph quoted as ‘“His hope of the next world was sure… Amen; even so, come, Lord Jesus!”’
findings.truth: Fabricated. The text reads ‘his hope will be sure, his faith steadfast’ and the closing words are ‘Amen; even so come, Lord Jesus!’ (no comma after ‘so’).

findings.claim: Question 4 mark scheme cites ‘Jane Rhys’s Wide Sargasso Sea’.
findings.truth: The author is Jean Rhys. The lesson body has it right; only the mark scheme was wrong.
findings.evidence: Wide Sargasso Sea (1966), Jean Rhys — named correctly in the same lesson’s content_html.

findings.claim: Flashcard [5]: the fire ‘removes Bertha, reduces Rochester’s power, and lets Jane inherit £20,000’.
findings.truth: The inheritance happens in ch.33, long before the fire, and is unconnected to it. Causal claim removed.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg ch.33; the fire is reported in ch.36.

findings.claim: ‘torn between passion (“Who in the world cares for you?” her conscience asks)’
findings.truth: In ch.27 that line is spoken by Feeling; Jane’s ‘conscience and reason turned traitors’ on the other side of the argument. Speaker corrected.

findings.claim: ‘This analytical depth is what separates Band 4–5 responses from lower bands.’
findings.truth: Invented band numbering. Replaced with the house wording ‘top-band responses’.

findings.claim: ‘Bronte’ without the diaeresis in nine flashcard questions (L1 ×2, L2 ×2, L5, L7, L8 ×3).
findings.truth: The author is Charlotte Brontë. Plain-text fields carry unicode. No instance of the ‘Brönte’ misspelling was found.
findings.evidence: Sweep of all eight raw files.

findings.claim: The ‘women feel just as men feel’ passage is repeatedly called Jane’s ‘rooftop speech’ (also in L4 and L8 mark schemes).
findings.truth: It is narration, not speech, and Jane is pacing the third-storey corridor when it comes — though she does climb to the leads earlier in the same chapter, so the shorthand is defensible. Left as is: renaming it would ripple through six fields and the narration in three lessons.

findings.claim: ‘Bertha Mason set fire to the house and died in the blaze.’
findings.truth: She died from the fall after jumping from the roof — as the very next sentence of the same paragraph says. Changed to ‘died that night’.

summary: Lesson 8 carried the exam damage: it named the board, claimed AO4/SPaG is assessed on the 19th-century novel question, marked the true answer wrong on the AO knowledge check, and gave 45 minutes instead of about 50. Four fabricated or misattributed quotations were found (Helen Burns's 'God of all' in two lessons, St John's closing line, and a Pride and Prejudice line given to Rochester), plus the fleet-wide error that all 48 practice questions were labelled 20 marks with a 20-mark ladder. Lesson 7 was clean apart from those fleet-wide labels and one spelling fix.
note_on_lesson_field: lesson 0 = the finding applies to all eight lessons.
